questions.stem: A 31 year old woman attends a fertility clinic after 18 months of trying to conceive. Her periods stopped 10 months ago. She has no nipple discharge and takes no medication. Her pregnancy test is negative and TSH normal. MRI shows a 6 mm pituitary lesion.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Prolactinoma is the commonest functioning adenoma (about half); in women it causes amenorrhoea and infertility, with or without galactorrhoea.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Amenorrhoea and infertility with a pituitary microadenoma; galactorrhoea is not required.

elim: Usually suprasellar and cystic, often in children, not a 6 mm intrasellar lesion.
Causes mass effects, usually large and late; a 6 mm lesion would not stop periods.
Oligomenorrhoea with hirsutism, no pituitary lesion.
High FSH from ovarian failure; does not explain the pituitary lesion.

steps.x: **E. Prolactinoma.** Amenorrhoea + infertility + microadenoma = prolactinoma.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man is referred with bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome. His wife says he snores and stops breathing at night. He has gained weight, sweats a lot and his tongue seems too big for his mouth. His BP is 158/96 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.e: GH excess causes soft tissue overgrowth: carpal tunnel, macroglossia, sleep apnoea, sweating, weight gain and hypertension.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Soft tissue overgrowth at several sites.

elim: Can cause carpal tunnel and macroglossia, but not sweating and coarse growth.
Causes carpal tunnel and weight gain, but with cold intolerance, not sweating.
Does not explain macroglossia or carpal tunnel.
Synovitis of small joints, not macroglossia.

steps.x: **A. Acromegaly.** Carpal tunnel + macroglossia + sleep apnoea = acromegaly.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has newly confirmed acromegaly with an IGF-1 three times the upper limit of normal. He has no bowel symptoms. His endocrinologist discusses screening for a cancer for which acromegaly increases his risk.
questions.q: Which cancer is he at most increased risk of?
questions.e: Acromegaly increases colorectal cancer risk (IGF-1 drives epithelial growth), so colonoscopic screening is offered.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: IGF-1 three times the upper limit
steps.x: GH/IGF-1 excess drives tissue growth, including colonic polyps.

elim: Linked to cirrhosis and hepatitis B and C.
Part of MEN type 2, not acromegaly.
Not the recognised acromegaly association.
Linked to smoking and ectopic hormones.

steps.x: **A. Colorectal cancer.** Acromegaly = colonoscopy for colorectal cancer risk.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has coarse facial features, enlarged hands and fatigue. Her IGF-1 is markedly raised. A full blood count and thyroid tests are sent.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding?
o: Normocytic anaemia with low free T4
questions.e: Acromegaly can cause a normocytic anaemia and hypothyroidism (from pituitary compression, so free T4 is low without a high TSH).

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
A pituitary macroadenoma affecting other axes.

elim: Primary hypothyroidism or B12 deficiency, not pituitary.
Iron deficiency, e.g. bleeding.
Not the pattern in acromegaly.
Thyrotoxicosis pattern.

steps.x: **C. Normocytic anaemia with low free T4.** Acromegaly: normocytic anaemia, hypothyroidism, colorectal cancer risk.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has central weight gain, purple striae and proximal weakness. Her overnight dexamethasone test is abnormal, plasma ACTH is high and cortisol suppresses on high-dose dexamethasone. MRI shows a 5 mm pituitary adenoma.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (about 20% of functioning tumours) causes Cushing's disease.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
ACTH-dependent cortisol excess from a pituitary adenoma.

elim: GH excess with coarse features and large hands.
ACTH would be suppressed.
Would not suppress on high-dose dexamethasone.
Occurs after bilateral adrenalectomy.

steps.x: **C. Cushing's disease.** ACTH-secreting pituitary tumour = Cushing's disease.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has a year of tiredness, cold intolerance, loss of body hair and reduced libido. His BP is 102/64 mmHg. MRI shows a 28 mm pituitary macroadenoma. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his results?
o: Hypopituitarism from compression by the adenoma
questions.e: A pituitary adenoma compressing the normal gland is the commonest cause of hypopituitarism: low cortisol, low T4 with inappropriately normal TSH, and low testosterone with low LH.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Several axes low with low or normal trophic hormones.

elim: ACTH would be high and he would be pigmented.
TSH would be high.
LH would be high.
Occurs in acute illness and does not explain low cortisol and testosterone.

steps.x: **A. Hypopituitarism from compression by the adenoma.** Low hormones + low/normal trophic hormones + macroadenoma = hypopituitarism.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with schizophrenia has taken risperidone for 3 years. She has amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and 4 months of worsening headaches. She has bitemporal field loss. Her prolactin is 9,800 mIU/L (<500) and MRI shows a 16 mm pituitary mass.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her raised prolactin?
questions.e: Antipsychotics raise prolactin, but a very high level with headaches, a field defect and a macroadenoma means a prolactinoma.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Drugs are a common confounder, but the mass and field defect need explaining.

elim: Can mildly raise prolactin, but does not cause a 16 mm mass.
Mildly raised prolactin at most, no mass.
Always exclude with beta-hCG, but it does not cause a field defect.
The classic distractor: drugs raise prolactin modestly and do not cause a mass or field loss.

steps.x: **D. Prolactinoma.** Very high prolactin + macroadenoma + field defect = prolactinoma, even on antipsychotics.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation (INR 5.2) has a sudden, severe headache behind his eyes and vomits. He had noticed blurred vision over the past year. He now has a drooping left eyelid. His BP is 96/60 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden retro-orbital headache and vomiting after prior visual problems, precipitated by coagulopathy, is pituitary apoplexy; low BP suggests acute ACTH loss.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: sudden, severe headache behind his eyes
blurred vision over the past year
steps.x: Haemorrhage into a pre-existing adenoma in an anticoagulated patient.

elim: Painful red eye with fixed mid-dilated pupil.
Not with ptosis and hypotension.
Can cause a third nerve palsy, but the prior visual symptoms and hypotension fit apoplexy.
Older patients with scalp tenderness and jaw claudication.

steps.x: **C. Pituitary apoplexy.** Previous visual symptoms + sudden retro-orbital headache = pituitary apoplexy.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman with a known 12 mm non-functioning pituitary adenoma is 34 weeks pregnant. She suddenly develops a severe headache behind both eyes, vomiting and worsening vision. Her BP is 118/74 mmHg and urine dipstick shows no protein.
questions.q: Which is the most likely precipitant of her presentation?
questions.e: Pregnancy is a precipitant of pituitary apoplexy (with surgery and coagulopathy): the gland enlarges in a confined sella and the adenoma can infarct or bleed.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
A known adenoma, pregnancy and sudden retro-orbital headache.

elim: Vomiting is a result, not the cause.
First trimester, and does not cause visual loss.
Does not explain worsening vision with a known adenoma.
Excluded by normal BP and no proteinuria.

steps.x: **E. Pregnancy-related enlargement of the pituitary.** Apoplexy precipitants: surgery, coagulopathy, pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman with a prolactinoma has had episodes of sweating, confusion and shaking before breakfast. During one, her capillary glucose was 2.1 mmol/L. Her corrected calcium is 2.84 mmol/L (2.2–2.6). She does not have diabetes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her hypoglycaemic episodes?
questions.e: Prolactinoma plus hypercalcaemia suggests MEN type 1; its pancreatic endocrine tumours include insulinoma, causing fasting hypoglycaemia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Pituitary + parathyroid = MEN1; now the pancreas.

elim: Hypoglycaemia is possible, but does not link the pituitary and calcium findings.
After gastric surgery, after meals.
She has no diabetes and the MEN1 picture explains it.
A microprolactinoma rarely causes it, and the calcium points to MEN1.

steps.x: **C. Insulinoma.** MEN1 = 3 Ps: parathyroid, pituitary, pancreas (insulinoma, gastrinoma).

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has acromegaly from a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma. His father had recurrent kidney stones and peptic ulcers. He has bone pain and feels thirsty. He is screened for an associated condition.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding?
questions.e: In MEN type 1, parathyroid hyperplasia or adenoma occurs in about 95%, giving primary hyperparathyroidism alongside pituitary prolactinoma or GH tumours.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: recurrent kidney stones and peptic ulcers
steps.x: Pituitary tumour plus a family history of stones and ulcers: MEN1.

elim: Malignancy or vitamin D excess.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency or CKD.
Conn's syndrome, not MEN1.
Medullary thyroid cancer in MEN2.

steps.x: **A. High calcium with high PTH.** MEN1: parathyroid in 95% (high calcium, high PTH).

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has an MRI for headaches that shows a 7 mm pituitary adenoma. Her endocrinologist explains that about three quarters of these tumours make a hormone. Blood tests are being arranged.
questions.q: Which hormone is the tumour most likely to secrete, if functional?
questions.e: About 75% of pituitary tumours are functional; of these about 50% secrete prolactin, 20% GH, 20% ACTH and 10% multiple hormones.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: three quarters of these tumours make a hormone
steps.x: Base rates of functioning adenomas.

elim: About 20% of functioning tumours.
About 20%.
Rare.
Made in the hypothalamus; adenomas do not secrete it.

steps.x: **C. Prolactin.** Prolactinoma is the commonest functioning adenoma.

questions.stem: A 50 year old bus driver has clipped wing mirrors on both sides several times this year. He has had morning headaches and nausea for 6 months. Fundoscopy is normal. His visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on visual field testing?
questions.e: A pituitary mass compressing the optic chiasm damages crossing nasal fibres, causing loss of both temporal fields (starting superiorly).

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: clipped wing mirrors on both sides
steps.x: Peripheral vision lost on both sides with mass-effect headaches.

elim: Optic nerve or macular disease, with reduced acuity.
Right optic tract or occipital lesion: loses one side only.
Left temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) lesion.
Glaucoma or a lateral chiasmal lesion.

steps.x: **A. Bitemporal hemianopia.** Hitting things on both sides = bitemporal hemianopia = chiasm.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman says her shoe size has gone up and her wedding ring no longer fits. Old photographs show her jaw and nose have enlarged. She has wrist pain and sweats a lot. Her BP is 150/92 mmHg and glucose 8.9 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Oral glucose tolerance test with GH
questions.e: IGF-1 is the initial test for suspected acromegaly and is also used to monitor disease activity; random GH is unreliable because it is pulsatile.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.
Suspected acromegaly: screen first.

elim: Images the tumour after biochemical confirmation.
The confirmatory test, after a raised IGF-1.
GH is pulsatile, so a single value is unreliable.
Assesses chiasm compression, not the diagnosis.

steps.x: **D. Serum IGF-1.** Acromegaly: IGF-1 first, then OGTT to confirm.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with a raised IGF-1 has an oral glucose tolerance test with growth hormone measured at baseline and every 30 minutes for 2 hours. GH chart (see item resources).

visual.title: GH during 75 g OGTT
visual.caption: GH does not suppress (normal nadir below 1 µg/L) and rises paradoxically.

questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation?
questions.e: Glucose normally suppresses GH; failure to suppress or a paradoxical rise confirms acromegaly.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.
Glucose should switch GH off.

elim: GH would be low throughout, and IGF-1 would be low.
The GH response is the point of this test.
GH would fall to almost undetectable.
A rise in glucose is the stimulus the test relies on.

steps.x: **A. Acromegaly confirmed.** OGTT: GH fails to suppress or rises = acromegaly.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has a 24 mm non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma found on MRI for headaches. On MRI it rises to touch the optic chiasm. She has not noticed any visual problems. Her pituitary blood tests are being sent.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional investigation?
questions.e: Formal visual field testing (perimetry) assesses chiasmal compression, which can be present without symptoms.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.

clues: rises to touch the optic chiasm
has not noticed any visual problems
steps.x: A mass at the chiasm needs field assessment, whatever the symptoms.

elim: Does not assess chiasmal function.
Tests retinal function.
Retinal vascular disease.
Acuity is often normal with chiasmal compression.

steps.x: **D. Formal visual field testing.** Any macroadenoma near the chiasm: formal visual fields.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has a CT head after a fall that incidentally shows a 9 mm pituitary lesion. He has no headaches, visual symptoms or features of hormone excess. His visual fields are full.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: Pituitary function tests: prolactin, IGF-1, cortisol, TSH and T4
questions.e: A pituitary incidentaloma needs laboratory tests to determine its functional status: full pituitary function including prolactin, IGF-1, cortisol and thyroid tests (then MRI).

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.

clues: incidentally shows a 9 mm pituitary lesion
steps.x: Incidental lesion: is it secreting, and is the rest of the gland working?

elim: Dangerous gold standard for hypopituitarism, not first.
Not done; diagnosis is by biochemistry and MRI.
Functional status must be checked first, and MRI is the imaging of choice.
Not indicated for a pituitary lesion.

steps.x: **C. Pituitary function tests: prolactin, IGF-1, cortisol, TSH and T4.** Incidentaloma: check function with pituitary bloods.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has had surgery for a pituitary macroadenoma. Her morning cortisol is borderline. Her endocrinologist wants the gold-standard test for adrenal and growth hormone reserve but notes she has epilepsy and ischaemic heart disease.
questions.q: Which test is the gold standard but must be avoided in her?
questions.e: The insulin tolerance test is the gold standard for hypopituitarism, but induced hypoglycaemia risks seizures, cardiac arrest and death, so it is contraindicated in epilepsy and heart disease.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.
A test using hypoglycaemia as the stress.

elim: Confirms acromegaly.
Screens for Cushing's.
A safer alternative for adrenal reserve, but not the gold standard.
Diagnoses diabetes insipidus.

steps.x: **A. Insulin tolerance test.** Hypopituitarism gold standard = insulin tolerance test (risk: seizures, cardiac arrest).

questions.stem: A 56 year old woman with known poor peripheral vision has a sudden severe headache behind her eyes and vomiting. She now has double vision. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg. A CT head is reported as showing a sellar mass without subarachnoid blood.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: MRI pituitary is the gold-standard imaging for pituitary tumours and confirms pituitary apoplexy (haemorrhage or infarction in the adenoma).

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must answer at this stage.

clues: sudden severe headache behind her eyes
steps.x: Suspected apoplexy: image the pituitary properly.

elim: Looks for an aneurysm; the sellar mass explains this.
For seizures.
For subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis.
Delays diagnosis; CT is less sensitive than MRI.

steps.x: **D. MRI pituitary.** Pituitary apoplexy is confirmed by MRI.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has acromegaly from a pituitary macroadenoma. He has severe heart failure and the anaesthetist judges him unfit for surgery. His IGF-1 remains high.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Somatostatin analogues such as octreotide inhibit GH secretion and are the first-line medical treatment for acromegaly, especially when surgery is not possible.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.
Acromegaly needing medical control.

elim: First-line for prolactinoma; only modestly effective in acromegaly.
Replacement for cortisol deficiency, not GH excess.
Thyroid replacement.
Definitive treatment, but he is unfit.

steps.x: **D. Octreotide.** Acromegaly medical treatment = somatostatin analogue (octreotide).

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has a 7 mm prolactinoma causing amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. Her prolactin is 3,200 mIU/L. Visual fields are normal. She would like to have children in the future.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Prolactinomas, micro or macro, are treated first-line with dopamine agonists (cabergoline or bromocriptine), which shrink the tumour and restore fertility.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.
Prolactinoma: medical treatment comes first, even before surgery.

elim: Treats symptoms of oestrogen lack, not the tumour or fertility.
For acromegaly.
Second-line for resistant disease.
First-line for most other pituitary tumours, but not prolactinoma.

steps.x: **B. Dopamine agonist (cabergoline).** Prolactinoma = dopamine agonist first.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has a 30 mm non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma with a bitemporal hemianopia. His prolactin is mildly raised at 1,100 mIU/L. His cortisol and thyroid function are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Non-functioning tumours with mass effect are treated mainly by transsphenoidal surgery; radiotherapy is kept for residual or recurrent disease.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.
A large non-secreting tumour threatening vision.

elim: Lowers prolactin from stalk compression but does not shrink a non-functioning tumour.
Unsafe with a field defect.
For GH-secreting tumours.
For residual or recurrent tumour after surgery.

steps.x: **E. Transsphenoidal surgery.** Non-functioning with mass effect = transsphenoidal surgery.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman had transsphenoidal surgery 6 months ago for a non-functioning macroadenoma. Her vision recovered. Follow-up MRI shows residual tumour in the cavernous sinus that has grown by 4 mm since the post-operative scan.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Radiotherapy is used for residual or recurrent pituitary tumour after surgery, particularly in the cavernous sinus where surgery cannot reach.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.

clues: residual tumour in the cavernous sinus
steps.x: Growing residual tumour after surgery.

elim: For prolactinomas.
Does not treat tumour growth.
Ongoing imaging is part of long-term care, especially with growth.
For GH-secreting tumours.

steps.x: **D. Radiotherapy.** Residual or recurrent tumour after surgery = radiotherapy.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has hypopituitarism from a macroadenoma. His 9am cortisol is 80 nmol/L, free T4 6.8 pmol/L with TSH 0.7 mU/L, and testosterone low. He is to start hormone replacement.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate order of replacement?
o: Growth hormone, then hydrocortisone, then testosterone
Testosterone and levothyroxine together, hydrocortisone only if unwell
questions.e: Replace cortisol first, then thyroxine, then sex hormones and GH. Thyroxine first speeds cortisol metabolism and can precipitate adrenal crisis.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.

clues: He is to start hormone replacement
steps.x: Several deficient axes, including cortisol.

elim: GH comes last.
Thyroxine before cortisol risks adrenal crisis.
Leaves dangerous cortisol deficiency.
Cortisol must come first.

steps.x: **B. Hydrocortisone, then levothyroxine, then testosterone.** Hypopituitarism: steroids before thyroxine.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man had transsphenoidal surgery for acromegaly a year ago. His hands and sweating have improved. He asks how his team will check whether the disease is still active.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term monitoring?
questions.e: Long-term care involves monitoring hormone levels and imaging; IGF-1 tracks acromegaly activity, and MRI looks for recurrence.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.

clues: surgery for acromegaly a year ago
steps.x: Monitoring after acromegaly treatment.

elim: For Cushing's.
Not relevant.
Pulsatile and unreliable on its own.
For prolactinoma.

steps.x: **D. Serum IGF-1 and pituitary MRI.** Acromegaly follow-up: IGF-1 and MRI.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with pituitary apoplexy confirmed on MRI has been given IV hydrocortisone. Over 6 hours his visual acuity falls from 6/9 to counting fingers and his visual fields are worsening. His BP is now 124/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Pituitary apoplexy is managed with urgent steroids and neurosurgical review; deteriorating vision needs surgical decompression of the chiasm.

steps.x: A management question: decide where in the pathway this patient is.
Steroids given, but chiasmal compression is getting worse.

elim: Medical treatment for prolactinoma, too slow here.
Not a treatment for chiasmal compression.
For acromegaly.
Waiting risks permanent blindness.

steps.x: **E. Urgent surgical decompression.** Apoplexy: steroids first; failing vision = surgical decompression.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has a pituitary adenoma removed. Histology shows a benign tumour of a single cell type that stains for growth hormone only. She asks whether her children are likely to inherit it.
questions.q: Which best describes the pathology of most pituitary adenomas?
o: Benign monoclonal proliferation of one anterior pituitary cell type
Hyperplasia of the whole pituitary in response to hypothalamic hormones
Malignant tumour of the posterior pituitary
questions.e: Adenomas are benign monoclonal growths of one anterior pituitary cell type; most are sporadic, with only rare genetic syndromes, so inheritance is unlikely.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.
One cell type, one hormone.

elim: Polyclonal, e.g. in pregnancy, not an adenoma.
Hypophysitis.
Adenomas are benign and anterior.
Rare, often affects the posterior pituitary with DI.

steps.x: **A. Benign monoclonal proliferation of one anterior pituitary cell type.** Adenoma = benign, monoclonal, one anterior cell type; mostly sporadic.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man with a slowly growing pituitary macroadenoma first notices that he cannot see objects in the upper outer parts of both visual fields. Later the whole temporal half of each field is lost.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the upper fields being affected first?
o: Compression of the optic radiation in the parietal lobe
Pressure from below on the inferior crossing nasal fibres of the chiasm
questions.e: The chiasm lies above the pituitary fossa. Suprasellar growth presses first on the inferior crossing nasal fibres, which serve the upper temporal fields: bitemporal superior quadrantanopia, then hemianopia.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.

clues: upper outer parts of both visual fields
whole temporal half of each field
steps.x: Bitemporal loss starting superiorly.

elim: Causes an inferior homonymous quadrantanopia.
Gives homonymous defects.
Enlarges the blind spot.
Unilateral, with flashes and a curtain.

steps.x: **C. Pressure from below on the inferior crossing nasal fibres of the chiasm.** Pituitary from below = superior quadrants first; craniopharyngioma from above = inferior.

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman with a prolactinoma starts cabergoline. Within 2 months her prolactin falls from 4,500 to 380 mIU/L and her periods return.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of cabergoline's effect?
o: Blocking prolactin receptors in the breast
Mimicking hypothalamic dopamine at D2 receptors on lactotrophs
questions.e: Prolactin is normally tonically suppressed by hypothalamic dopamine; dopamine agonists restore that inhibition and shrink prolactinomas.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.
Dopamine is the brake on prolactin.

elim: Would not lower prolactin levels.
Not how it lowers prolactin.
Octreotide's action.
TRH stimulates prolactin.

steps.x: **C. Mimicking hypothalamic dopamine at D2 receptors on lactotrophs.** Prolactin is held down by dopamine; cabergoline is a dopamine agonist.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man has acromegaly. His growth hormone is high, but his clinician explains that most of the soft tissue overgrowth and the insulin resistance are not caused by GH acting directly.
questions.q: Which mediator is mainly responsible?
questions.e: Excess GH drives IGF-1 production in the liver, which mediates most somatic growth and metabolic effects of acromegaly.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.

clues: not caused by GH acting directly
steps.x: GH works largely through a second messenger hormone.

elim: Drives cortisol, not soft tissue growth.
Stimulates GH release upstream.
Causes galactorrhoea and hypogonadism.
Inhibits GH.

steps.x: **C. IGF-1 from the liver.** GH acts through liver IGF-1.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has pituitary apoplexy. Two hours after arrival she is drowsy and her BP falls to 82/50 mmHg. Her sodium is 128 mmol/L and glucose 3.4 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her deterioration?
o: Acute ACTH deficiency causing adrenal insufficiency
questions.e: Haemorrhage into the adenoma can compromise ACTH secretion, precipitating acute adrenal insufficiency: hypotension, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia. Hence urgent steroids.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.
Shock, low sodium and low glucose after apoplexy.

elim: Does not cause hypoglycaemia.
Causes hypernatraemia, not 128 mmol/L.
Not the usual mechanism.
No infection source, and the triad fits cortisol lack.

steps.x: **A. Acute ACTH deficiency causing adrenal insufficiency.** Apoplexy can cause acute adrenal insufficiency: give hydrocortisone now.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with a known pituitary macroadenoma has a sudden severe headache and vomiting. His right eye now looks down and out with a drooping eyelid and dilated pupil. MRI shows haemorrhage within the adenoma.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his eye signs?
o: Compression of the oculomotor nerve in the cavernous sinus
Raised intracranial pressure causing a sixth nerve palsy
questions.e: Sudden swelling from haemorrhage in a confined sella compresses the optic chiasm and the cavernous sinus, where the third nerve runs.

steps.x: A mechanism question: link the finding to the underlying physiology.

clues: looks down and out with a drooping eyelid
steps.x: A third nerve palsy from lateral spread of a suddenly swollen adenoma.

elim: No other brainstem signs; the MRI explains it.
Fatigable, no pupil involvement.
Causes field loss, not ophthalmoplegia.
Would give a convergent squint, not ptosis and dilated pupil.

steps.x: **B. Compression of the oculomotor nerve in the cavernous sinus.** Apoplexy: chiasm (fields) + cavernous sinus (III, IV, VI palsies).
